text: Question five. What is a deadlock, and what four conditions cause it? A deadlock is a set of threads, each waiting forever for something another one holds. Two threads, two locks. The first takes A, then wants B. The second takes B, then wants A. If both take their first lock before either takes its second, each waits on the other, for good. Coffman's four conditions all have to hold. Mutual exclusion: a lock has one holder at a time. Hold and wait: a thread keeps one lock while it waits for another. No preemption: nothing can take a lock away. And circular wait: a cycle of threads, each waiting on the next. Break any one, and the deadlock can't happen. Question six. How do you prevent deadlocks in practice? Go after the conditions, one at a time. Circular wait is the usual target: every thread takes its locks in one global order, A before B. Now whichever thread gets A also gets B, and the other waits holding nothing. No schedule deadlocks. No preemption: take a lock with a timeout, so a thread that can't get its second lock gives up, releases its first, and tries again. Hold and wait: one coarse lock instead of several, so no thread holds one while it waits for another. Mutual exclusion: share nothing. Give the state one owner thread and send it work through a queue, so no other thread needs a lock on it. And keep critical sections short, so contention stays low. One catch: threads that time out and retry in lockstep can collide forever. That's livelock, in the quick round.
